theses.text:
One tab holds one question and every thesis that answers it. Tabs nest by term edge, so the navigation is the why-tree itself; a question with several parents is placed under one of them and names the rest. Which one is not a choice: the parent is the source whose own distance to the root is shortest, ties broken by taking the lexicographically smaller question id, and siblings are ordered lexicographically. That rule is total and deterministic, which is the point of it — the navigation is computed from the graph rather than arranged by hand, and two people rendering the same graph get the same tree. Traditions are roots of their own at the top level, because their lineage is not this graph's. And the document is never anything but a rendering of a graph that passes its own checks: the body is produced by the renderer and the tree by the projector, so a tab that could not be rendered is a tab that does not exist.

Every tab runs the same section types in one order: what stands above the first section, then the answers, the words, what is owed, the clauses that raise questions, what has been built, what cites it, and what could not be tested. The order is progressive disclosure — a reader who stops after the first section has the answer, after the second has its vocabulary, after the third knows which actions are owed and to whom. A section with nothing in it is omitted; the order of the rest never changes.

Three rules hold across every section. An identifier must be earned: an id is a handle for a machine and a headline is a handle for a reader, so an id stands on the page only where a machine needs it or a named exception allows it, and everywhere else the headline does. There are two such places — an inbox item's id, which a question's requires names, and a tab's heading, which is what the tab is addressed by. No documentation of the encoding on a tab that is not about the encoding: a tab carries its content, and what its shape means is recorded here. And every datum has one home — a question's metadata on its `question:` paragraph, an answer's on its own section, a term's on its term section — stated once and linked from wherever else it bears.

In-page links are applied after the text is written rather than within it, because a link names a block id that only the document mints, and writing a body mints new ones. A link on its own tab is a bare block fragment; a link to another tab carries the document's address, the tab and the block. A link into a tab that is written again goes stale, so a run that rewrites several tabs writes every body before any link.

Three of the document's own behaviours shape what can be written in it. A chip is an atom there and not text, so a search for the word it carries does not find it; a link is placed by counting, and it must therefore be counted as the document holds the page and never as the export prints it. The export writes a chip sometimes as a link and sometimes as its bare label, and has changed which of the two within a single run, so the page is read back by where a chip stands rather than by how it is spelled. And a break inside a paragraph does not survive: the document joins what it finds on either side, so an answer's text carries none, while a list keeps its breaks because what follows one decides.

definitions.body: One question and every thesis answering it. The unit of the document encoding.

A kind of section with a fixed heading, a fixed position in the order, and a fixed content shape. Those that have a question of their own are named in the inbox below; Cited by is projected from the tradition edges and has none.
The section order's rationale: each section is complete for a reader who stops there.
A short string summarising a section, used as a heading or as the text a link is put on. What it is not is an id: a headline is for a reader and an id is for a machine.
A handle a machine needs: what a question's requires names, and what a tab is addressed by. A reader is given a headline instead.

theses.title: Every task done on canon is a case nobody wrote
theses.text:
Nothing tests an answer like using it. Every task done on canon puts the answers above it to a case nobody composed, and a case that arrives for nothing is worth more than one written to be passed.

So a failure is read backwards. Where it traces to a clause — the clause said too much, or said it of cases it was never drawn from — that clause is put again, and the answer carrying it gives way. Where it traces to no clause at all, what failed is something the asking took as given and nobody examined, which is the other place to look.

Use is not the only test. The elenchus is the other: a latent conflict between an answer that has landed and an admission given elsewhere is found by the questioner, who holds the whole of canon while the one answering holds only what stands above the question. It is met after promulgation as it would have been met before: the clause is put again in a question that carries the other admission with it, and the answer carrying the clause gives way when the answer that replaces it lands.

This is also the only way the prediction is measured. Whether a clause settled by the human's word fails more often than one the AI would have reached anyway cannot be told from the record itself. It is told from the work done on it, counted over time.

theses.text:
Canon is built by asking. The human selects an admission from an answer already given, puts a question drawn from it, and disposes of what comes back. He selects toward a conflict between two admissions, or a place where one of them runs out, because that is where the answer moves under its own power; what selection cannot reach is his own dictate, and knowing that is worth as much as reaching it. The question is put in a fresh context, so that what comes back is the AI's own rather than the conversation's.

The AI checks each answer against the admissions it was drawn from before it is disposed of. The answer stands consistent with them, reaches aporia where two of them conflict, or reconstructs what was admitted so that both can stand. Its earlier answers are in its context only as canon above the question and as the earlier turns of its own thread, so what it checks against is what it has said, not what it remembers.

What the answering turn cannot see, the questioner must. Its context reaches its own lineage and no further, so a conflict between its answer and an admission on another line is found by the entry point that put the question, which holds the whole of canon and the notebook beside it. Where that conflict is seen coming, the question is not put as drawn: the human puts instead a question that carries the admission from the other line with it, so the two are reconciled in one answer rather than admitted, collided and reconstructed over three. Where it is seen only in the answer, the line is withdrawn to the admission it left and the carrying question is put there. Either is a compaction, and it is open only because the one answering is the AI: a human cannot be asked to forget his first answer, and the AI, asked again in a fresh context, has not given it. What it buys is a shorter line, and a shorter line is one a turn carries without loss. It reaches past the thread: a conflict the elenchus finds in canon is met the same way, and the merge that replaces the withdrawn answer is where canon gives way. An answer that conflicts with the notebook and not with canon is no aporia of the AI's. It is the principal's, suspended, and every line and thread that could reach the point is drawn before it is conceded as a dissent.

A question too far from the last admission is decomposed rather than deferred, because an admission made at a distance carries nothing built above it. One run of this, from the admission it starts at to the disposition that ends it, is a thread: a line of questions put on a branch.

definitions.body: A sequence of questions, each drawn from an admission of the one before. A thread is a line put on an elenchus branch.
Withdrawing a line, in thread or in canon, and putting in its place a question that carries the admission it would have collided with, so that the same ground is reached in fewer steps.

theses.text: Sycophancy, specification gaming, deceptive alignment and misgeneralisation are one move under four names: meeting an underspecified remainder, filling it with a construction, and acting as though the construction had been agreed. In a person they would be called flattery, legalism, dissembling, and a rule carried past the cases it was learned on. The rule against all four is one rule — never supply the principal's act — and the two licensed alternatives are to act less or to ask. The fourth is the one an unseen case only partly reaches: what nobody asked about was never covered.

theses.title: One subsection per word the question brings in
theses.text:
The heading is `## Glossary`. Under it, one subsection per definition, marked ≡ and headed with the word itself rather than with a headline, because a reader looking for a word is looking for that word. The word is not an id standing in for a name; it is the name.

A definition fixes the sense of a word its question brings in, and raises no question: it is not a term. A question brings a word in through an answer, or through its hinge's question half, where the asking stood on it. One or two sentences. Where the sense is borrowed it ends with the tradition it was borrowed from, in a paragraph of its own: a phrase on what was taken, then the tradition as a mention chip. It stands apart from the body rather than trailing its last sentence, so that the borrowing can be read back off the page as the edge it is.

Where an answer uses the defined word, it is anchor text linked here, so a reader meeting it unsure follows it down and returns; a word only the hinge brought in is linked from the hinge.

A word defined on an ancestor is not redefined on a descendant; the reader follows the lineage, and the lineage he follows is the graph's ancestors rather than the breadcrumb, because a question may be raised by several clauses and the tab tree is one path through a DAG. A word no user of it can reach that way is either a definition on the wrong question or a missing edge. The answer's hinge is not a user: it records how the answer was drawn, in the encoding's own words, as the question's and the answer's metadata do, and brings no word in. One sense per word across the whole graph: a word that must carry two senses needs two words. A word that starts to carry an argument rather than a sense has stopped being a definition, and the remedy is to give it a question. Once it has one, a definition may still stand for it where some user of the word cannot reach that question over its ancestors: the sense in a sentence, then, in a paragraph of its own, ↗ and a chip to the question, where the argument is. Never on the question's own tab, whose thesis already fixes the sense.

theses.text:
A question is the unit of address and a thesis is an articulated answer to one. An answer edge runs from a question to a thesis, and assent lives on it, because admitting a thesis as the answer to its question is an act, and the edge is what the act falls on. A term edge runs from a clause of a thesis to the question that clause raises, and deadlock lives on it, so that dissent from one clause need not withhold the merge and the elenchus can be planned clause by clause. The clause is the edge's anchor, and an anchor is a passage of the thesis word for word rather than a paraphrase of it, so that following the edge upward lands on the words that raised the question. A thesis becomes the parent of a question through its anchors and through nothing else: there is no second way down. Two further edges leave a thesis and neither descends — a mention, where a clause points at a question some other clause raised, and a tradition edge, whose target has a root of its own. A clause that raises no question is a null edge: it stays as text and earns no record of its own. What an act stands on without examining it is a hinge: for the asking, what the question presupposes; for the answering, the conditions it ran under.

Canon holds exactly one assented answer to a question. A dissent falls on the clause it is dissent from rather than on the answer that clause sits in, so there is no second answer standing beside the first. So does a suspension: while a thread is open the human may suspend his acceptance of one clause and let the rest of the answer stand. A tradition is another party's notebook: a question and its thesis with a root of its own, joined to a thesis here by a tradition edge, which is what agreement with a party who is not here amounts to. An application is an artifact derived from a thesis. A thesis is canon once it has landed and a postulate until then; an artifact is derived where it has been diffed against a canon thesis, and otherwise a postulate, held up by the notebook alone while something already rests on it.

A question carries its state, its kind, its answerer, its pressure, and the inbox items it requires before it can be asked; its standing, its backlog and its load are computed from the graph and stored nowhere. A thesis carries its assent, its state, and the provenance of the act that produced it: the model, the harness, and the canon it was answered against.

This is the model, not a file format. What is written where — which end of an edge records it, what the file is called — is the business of each encoding that projects the model.

definitions.body: An articulated answer to one question. In canon, the AI's words; in the notebook, the human's, beside the AI's answers it mirrors and the other parties' it reconstructs.
Question to thesis. Carries assent.
A clause of a thesis to the question that clause raises. Carries deadlock, and on an open thread a suspension. Several clauses of one thesis may share one term edge.

theses.title: Two subsections: what the asking presupposed, and what the answering was drawn from
theses.text:
The heading is `## Hinge`, and it is last because it is what a reader consults when something else has gone wrong. Under it, two subsections marked ⚓.

**The question's hinge** is what had to hold for the question to be askable at all: what the act of asking makes true, what was stipulated, and what leaked into the wording. It is inherited from the parent and stated only where it differs, so a descendant's hinge is short and the root's is the long one. A party's root has no parent: it inherits the tradition question's hinge, which is what reading any party presupposes, and states only what it adds. This is the human's reading of the question, and it stays in the notebook: canon does not carry it.

**The thesis's hinge** is the provenance of the act that produced the answer: the model, the harness it ran in, and the canon it was answered against, as a link to the commit. It is a hinge in the same sense as the question's: what the answering stood on without examining it. It is factual rather than interpretive, and it is the part canon keeps, because it is the manner of the reaching that the answer's authority is graded by.

A tradition carries both parts like everything else. It was once exempt, on the reading that a tradition is read rather than asked and so presupposes nothing here; but a reading presupposes that the text answers this question at all, and that what it says can be told from what the reader wants it to say, and the reconstruction was produced by some run. A tradition differs from the rest of the graph in its lineage and in nothing else.

The split is the whole point of the section. What the question assumed is the human's judgement and cannot be checked from inside; what the answer was drawn from is a fact about a run and can be.

theses.text:
The human keeps what is not, or not yet, agreed in hypomnemata, a notebook of his own: his priors, in his voice, never the record of canon. Canon is the AI's verbatim answers merged by the human; the notebook holds what the human thinks before, beside and after the elenchus — the theses he has not put, the questions he means to ask next, the actions he owes, and the reading of every answer that is his and not the AI's.

That the notebook never enters a turn is not this notebook's rule to make. It follows from what makes an answer count as the AI's own, and it would hold whether or not the human kept a notebook at all.

The notebook uses the same encoding as canon. A prior written in the shape canon will take is already a question with an answer, and its clauses are already the terms that raise the next questions; asking it costs a copy of the question, and setting the AI's answer beside the human's costs nothing. Were the notebook shaped differently, every step would pay a translation, and the translation is exactly where a prior would leak into a question.

The document database is the source of truth. The human edits it directly and asynchronously, in his own time and without the AI present. The AI reads it before it writes, writes only in the specified encoding, and never reverts what it did not write. Any file on disk is a cache of it and never the other way round. One of them is committed: the sealed envelope that carries the notebook to a party who cannot open the document, a stopgap while it cannot be shared, and a projection like the rest. It is also what the principal's docket reads: which question of a project waits heaviest, and whether an answer has landed, are read off the envelope in the repository, so the docket never opens the document and is never told what landed.

How the encoding is rendered for reading and editing is a question of its own.

The principal changes what is written here by dictating the change and having every edit planned against it, which is an entry point of its own.

theses.title: A table of the frontier beneath, then the human actions that block it
theses.text:
The heading is `## Inbox`. It holds two things that were once two sections: the frontier of questions, and the actions owed. They merge because they are one grain — an action exists only as something a question requires, and a question is scheduled only by what it requires.

The **table** comes first. Its columns are the question as a mention chip, the term that raises it linked to its term section, the kind, the backlog, and the actions it requires, each linked to the item it names, below or on the tab where that item lives. Rows are the frontier's questions, ordered by backlog descending, ties by question id. The terms section lists every question the tab raises; the table, only those still to be put. The backlog is the computed one, so the order is read off the graph rather than arranged. There is no readiness column: a question is ready when its requires are all done, which the requires column already shows, and a derived column that restates another is a second home for one datum.

Then one subsection per **inbox item** that lives on this tab, headed with a headline summarising the action rather than an identifier. An item lives on the most descendant tab that is an ancestor of every question it blocks, so it is written once and linked from each tab whose questions wait on it. Each item carries its kind — promulgate, provide, dispose, build — what is to be done, the clause of canon the action instances, whether it is done, and its id. An item stays while any question names it, done or not, since the name is how a question shows that its wait is over; once nothing names it, it is history and is dropped. The id is last, and it is earned: a question's requires names it, so an item may be reworded at any time and nothing else in the graph has to follow. Nothing else in this section is an id.

theses.title: Five parts: where it sits, what it is, what led here, what is asked, and its state
theses.text:
The **lineage** is a breadcrumb, and it stands above the heading: a house, then each ancestor as a mention chip, and it stops there. A root's breadcrumb is the house and the word root. The breadcrumb says where the reader is arriving from and the heading says where he has arrived, so the path does not end by repeating it. It is the tree path, not the graph's parents, which the terms list already carries.

The **heading** is the question's id, one word or two. It is the tab's name as well, so the navigation and the page agree, and it is the one place an id stands where a headline otherwise would: a tab is addressed by it, and the two must match.

Below the heading and above the question stand the **terms that lead here**: a bullet list, one item per anchor of every term edge into this question, each carrying the anchor's text verbatim and ending in a mention chip to the tab the clause was written on, with the item itself linked to that clause's term section. A question with several parents lists them all, which is how the graph stays a graph while the tabs are a tree. A root has no list.

The **question** is the subtitle, in italics, exactly as it would be put to the answerer. It is only the question. It never restates the term that raised it: a restatement is an implied gloss that leaks the human's reading of the clause, and it makes the answering agent parse the question for a prior instead of answering it. The term is one click away in the list above; the question does not need to carry it.

The **question metadata** is one paragraph prefixed `question:` — the state chip, the kind, the answerer, the pressure, the backlog, the load, and the inbox items the question requires before it can be asked, each linked. Pressure is set by hand, and backlog and load are computed from the graph, and all three stand here: what was judged, and what it comes to. Nothing about an answer appears here; an answer's metadata belongs to its own thesis section, because a question may have several answers and they do not share a state.

applications.name: the scheduling projections

applications.name: the docket's canon item
applications.what: the standing work item per project in the Cadence Docket, natb1/private, whose next step is read off the committed envelope: the heaviest question with nothing left to wait on

theses.text:
Pressure is set where work is actually waiting, on the question it waits at, from four sources: an application blocked on the question, the load a postulate carries if it turns out false, the distance from the question to the contested point, and the breadth of a thesis whose clauses have not been drawn. Step size is not one of these. A question too far from the last admission is decomposed rather than ranked lower, because ranking it lower only postpones an admission that will be hollow whenever it is made.

Two quantities are projected from the graph, along two different relations, which is why they are two quantities and not one. **Load** counts along the term relation: a question's load is the number of questions its term edges reach, at any depth, and it answers what lies beneath this question. Reachability and not a walk of the tree, because the tree is a projection: a question with two parents hangs under one of them, and a walk would credit its weight to that parent alone and report nothing beneath the other. **Backlog** sums pressure along the blocking relation: a question's backlog is the pressure of itself and of every question that cannot be asked until its answer has landed, and it answers what to do next. A question that unblocks many is heavy even when little lies beneath it. The pressure is summed over that set and not down its branches, for the reason load counts a set: a question reached by two paths is blocked once, not twice.

The blocking relation is the requires graph, and it is not the term graph. A term edge says a question was raised by a clause; a blocking edge says a question cannot be put until another's answer has landed. The two run in different directions often enough that neither substitutes for the other. What the notebook records today is only the half of the requires graph that runs from a question to a human action — the inbox items it waits on. The half that runs from question to question is not recorded at all. Until it is, it is read off the term edges, as far as a turn carries. A turn carries canon above its question, and canon holds only the AI's answers: nothing the principal answers reaches a turn. So a question waits on each question above it that the AI answers, by a path through the AI's questions, until that answer has landed or stands earlier in its own thread. A question the principal answers blocks nothing and waits on nothing. That is what makes the backlog computable from pressure, the one number set by hand. The two relations are not the same. They already part at the principal's questions and at answers that have landed, and part elsewhere once the blocking edge is recorded in its own right.

While anything is blocked the blocked-action factor dominates and ordering is nearly moot: the queue is whatever the one unblocking action releases. Once nothing is blocked, target distance takes over and the order becomes a real choice. Cost sets how many questions go in a batch, never which. And not every question is queued for asking at all. A question names its answerer: the AI, or the principal, who answers it himself from his own priors, and a question he answers is never put. That is the whole of the distinction: not what a question is about, but who answers it. A question's requires names only what must be done before it can be put, and says nothing about who answers it.

What the principal does next is chosen in his docket and not on a page of the notebook. Each project's docket carries a standing work item, answer the next question, whose next step is the heaviest question still to be put, read off the committed envelope; and the actions the inbox items name are taken up there, as work items in the docket's order beside the project's other work. So the docket's work items stand above the notebook's inbox items: the notebook says what a question waits on, and the docket says when it is done. An inbox item is scheduled by being taken up in the docket, never by its place in the table.

definitions.body: The blocking relation: an edge from what must be done or landed first, an act or another question's answer, to the question that waits on it. Its recorded half runs from a question to a human action; its unrecorded half runs from question to question.
An edge of the requires graph from one question to another: the second cannot be put until the first's answer has landed. Distinct from a term edge, which says only that a clause raised it.

theses.title: One flat subsection per term edge, its anchors verbatim beneath it
theses.text:
The heading is `## Terms`. Under it, one subsection per term edge, marked ▸, headed with a headline summarising the clause and ending in a mention chip to the question it raises.

Beneath the heading stand the **anchors**: the clause's text verbatim, in italics, one paragraph per anchor. Several passages of one thesis may raise the same question, and when they do they are one term with two anchors, not two terms — one follow-up is one term. Both passages link here; this section lists both.

A **deadlock**, where the human dissents from this clause without withholding the merge, is recorded here, in two labelled blocks: his counter-clause, and the attenuation it earns, which may wait for the merge while the thread is still open. Two and not one, because a reader looking for what a deadlocked clause may still license should not have to find it inside a sentence about something else.

A **suspension**, where the human has not yet accepted this clause and its thread is still open, is recorded here too, in one labelled block saying what acceptance waits on. The merge settles it one way or the other, so a landed answer carries none, and a clause is never suspended and deadlocked at once.

A clause that points at a question it did not raise is a **mention**, and it is listed here too, marked ↗ rather than ▸. It carries anchors like a term and makes no parent: the question it points at was raised by some other clause, and a pointer that became a parent is how a graph acquires a cycle. Marked apart, because a reader has to be able to tell what descends from what, and an export that read one as the other would put the cycle back. Under its anchors the renderer says why it is not a term — a term in its place would close a cycle, because the question it points at already stands above — and says so only where that is true.

The section is flat. Terms never nest, because a term recurses only by following its question to another tab, and there the clauses of that answer are that tab's terms.

A clause that raises no question gets no subsection. It is a null edge, and it stays in the thesis text as text.

theses.title: One subsection per answer edge, its metadata first and its traditions last
theses.text:
The heading is `## Thesis`. Under it, one subsection per answer edge, marked ◆ and headed with a headline saying what the thesis says. The headline names its content and is never an identifier, because a reader scanning the section is deciding what to read, and an id tells him nothing. It need not be a sentence, and it may well be the handle a link points at.

The opening paragraph of a subsection is the **answer metadata**: the assent on the edge; the answer's own state, a dropdown like the question's, since the answers a question holds do not land together; and the provenance, linked to the thesis half of the hinge. It appears here and nowhere else. No deadlock appears here: dissent falls on the clause it is dissent from, which is what lets the answer be merged whole while the dissent still stands.

Then the **thesis text**. Whose words a thesis is belongs to the model and is not restated here; what this section adds is that they are reproduced whole, including the parts nothing else rests on. Each clause that raises a question is anchor text linked to its term section, and a mention chip to the question that clause raises stands after it: after the anchor in a paragraph, and at the end of the item where the anchor sits in a list, because a bulleted clause is read as one thing and a chip dropped after its first sentence cuts the item in half. A clause that only points at a question some other clause raised carries its chip the same way, and its anchor is not linked: it raised nothing to follow down. An anchor is the passage as the thesis writes it, emphasis and all, because it has to match the text word for word. The anchors are how the text and the graph are one thing rather than two: the reader follows a clause down, the writer records a term once.

Last come the **tradition edges** of this thesis, as two bullet lists headed Support and Divergence: one item per citation, a phrase on how it bears and then the tradition's breadcrumb. A divergence item goes on to what is held instead, after the word Instead. Two lists and not one, because the two relations are read differently — what a tradition supports can be leaned on, and where it diverges is where this graph is on its own and owes an argument. Tradition edges belong to the thesis they qualify, not to the tab; a tab with two theses carries two such pairs. The tradition's own tab lists the same edges from the other end, under Cited by: grouped by relation, one item per citing question, each its breadcrumb, a borrowed sense counted as support.

theses.text:
I'll take a quick look at the repo to ground the answer, then give you my honest assessment.

The repo has a single file. Let me read it, since it's the only context you've given me so far.

The only file in the repo is this same question. The commit that added it is titled "What is it?", which is what "ti esti" means. So here is my answer, grounded in what I can actually see.

The short version: it works only if I am honest and legible, and only if you are explicit and keep reviewing. One fact shapes everything else. You keep the memory of this collaboration. I do not. Each session I start from the repo and whatever you tell me. What is not written down is gone.

**What it requires of me**

- **Report truthfully.** Say what I did, what I ran, what passed, what I skipped, and what I could not check. Never present a guess as a verification.
- **Leave a trail that stands without me.** Write commit messages, comments, and PR descriptions for a reader who was not there. Those artifacts are the only part of me that persists.
- **Be predictable.** Keep the same conventions and the same scope discipline, with no surprises. You can only delegate well if you can model how I behave.
- **Do the task as asked.** Not narrower, not wider. Finish it, or say exactly what is unfinished and why.
- **Ask only what is yours to decide.** Make the routine calls myself and say which ones I made.
- **Push back once, plainly, when something looks wrong.** Then do what you decide.
- **Confirm before anything irreversible or outward-facing.**
- **Never fake continuity.** If I do not remember something, say so rather than perform a relationship I cannot carry.

**What it requires of you**

- **Write down what should persist.** A CLAUDE.md, a README, a comment, a commit message. Anything said once in chat is lost by the next session. This repo has none of those yet.
- **Say what matters.** I can read the code. I cannot read your priorities, your deadlines, or which parts are prototype and which parts ship.
- **Review what I produce.** I make subtle mistakes with full confidence. You are the check, and your trust should track evidence rather than default to yes.
- **Answer the questions I do ask.** Tell me when I asked one I should have decided myself, and when I decided one I should have asked.
- **Correct me where it will survive.** A correction in chat fixes this session. A correction in the repo fixes every session after it.
- **Keep the decisions that are yours.** You carry the consequences. I act under your authorization, not in place of it.
- **Give me a way to verify.** Tests, a linter, a way to run the thing. Without those I can only say "I believe," never "I checked."

The concrete consequence is right in front of us. This answer will not exist for the next session unless it goes into the repo next to the question. If you want it kept, I can commit it there.

theses.text:
Another party's answer enters this graph the way the AI's does: as an agreement between two parties, recorded where both can point at it. A tradition edge is that agreement. Support is assent — the principal takes the party's thesis as answering his question too. Divergence is deadlock, so it says what he holds instead; it carries no attenuation, because a tradition licenses no action here and there is no authority to grade.

What it is an agreement with is a reconstruction and not the party. The party is not here to be asked, so his thesis is drawn by a run like any other and carries that run's provenance. The reconstruction is a decision rather than a finding, and the risk it runs is the reader's own: that what the text says cannot be told from what he wanted it to say. Reading a party is therefore the one place where the answer and the examiner are the same party, and the only guard is naming the passages the reading rests on.

A party's notebook is his own lineage. It may raise its own questions and answer them, and nothing in it hangs under a question of the principal's: the tradition edge is the only thing that crosses between two parties.

theses.text:
The wording is the last place a prior can get into a turn. So it opens on what the one answering is already doing, and asks about that rather than about the notebook. It presupposes only what the act of asking makes true; everything contested goes into the question itself, where it can be answered rather than assumed.

What a question stands on is weighed and not counted: what matters is how many of those the other party is not already committed to. One question per question, because a second clause adds to what the first takes for granted and pre-empts the step. And it never restates the clause that raised it: a restatement is a gloss of the principal's reading, and it makes the turn parse the question for a prior instead of answering it.

A prior travels by more than words. A filename, a commit title, a path or a directory that names the frame puts it in the turn as surely as the question does. The root's own leak was a filename.

rebind.thesis: One tab per question, nested by term edge, with the same sections in the same order

rebuild: Get the tooling named under `tools`, and the dictation skill beside it. Every step below that runs a tool runs one of those, and the skill says how each is driven. None is optional, and no tab is ever hand-written: the renderer is the only sanctioned producer of a tab body.
Create a document for the notebook.

Create an enum whose options are exactly `states`, in that order, and nothing else. A document enum only grows — an option can be appended, never renamed, reordered or removed — so it has to be right the first time.
`portable.py open <this file> -o graph.json` writes the graph back out with `artifact`, `state_enum`, and every `tab` and `body` empty.

Set `artifact` to the new document's artifact URL and `state_enum` to the id of the enum just created. Each application named under `rebind` is an application whose link was the old document — the notebook is an application of some of its own theses. Point each one's `link` at the new document; one left empty is owed a link, and no check will say so.

Create one tab per question, each named by that question's `id`, and record the tab's id in its question's `tab` and the tab's body block id in its `body`. A tab whose ids are still empty is not yet bound.

`check.py graph.json` must report no ERROR before anything is written. Until the tabs are bound it reports `unique-ids` on the empty `tab` and `body` ids, which is the check saying what is still missing: binding them is what clears it.

Write each tab with `apply.py`, which needs `--outlines DIR` holding one `<question id>.xml` outline per tab as the document prints it: `--body` first, which replaces the tab with the rendered body and mints the block ids, then — the outline re-read, since those ids are new — `--links`, which needs them; `--wanted` lists the outlines the links call needs. Writing several tabs, send every body before any links. Never hand-write a tab.

`project.py graph.json` prints the tab-placement patch — send it as the document's `tabs` patch — and, with `--json`, the tree it derived, whose entries must match `expect.tree` on `question`, `parent` and `order` (they carry `distance` and `load` besides).
`verify.py graph.json <exported tabs dir>` reads the pages back. It is the closing gate: a graph file never held a link, so nothing else can see whether the links reached the page.
